newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-House of Fraser sees more job cuts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-House of Fraser sees more job cuts.

text.p: Struggling British department store group House of Fraser Plc said on Monday it was axing around 1,000 jobs in a big cost-cutting drive and saw scope for more savings, including possible further job losses.

The restructuring by the company, dubbed House of Horrors' by some London retail analysts, involves three store disposals and a clear-out of unwanted stock. The company said the move was expected to save around 10 million pounds ($16 million) a year, but added there would be more to come.

The retailer estimated the total cost of the job cuts, disposals and stock clearance at between 41 and 49 million pounds. This was in line with estimates last October, when chief executive John Coleman outlined plans for a shake up to try and improve the firm's dismal performance since the Fayed brothers, owners of Harrods, floated the company in 1994.
Coleman said there were more costs to come out of the business and the firm was looking at ways to improve operating efficiencies in its stores.

"You have to say when you're trying to improve efficiency and you're looking for ways to save money...there's always the likelihood or possibility of maybe further job losses," he told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Coleman was hopeful of selling the three stores -- an Army & Navy store in Eastbourne on the south coast, and House of Fraser Sheffield and Binns in Scunthorpe both in the north of England. He said the firm was keen to sell them as going concerns and preserve jobs.

The three were identified as having little chance of returning to an acceptable level of profitability. Coleman said there were other problem stores in the group, but would not say which ones. Last October, House of Fraser warned it could close between five and 10 of its 51 shops.
In afternoon trade, House of Fraser shares stood a penny higher at 143. They were floated at 180 pence in April 1994.
The retailer has been plagued by problems since its stock market float and made a loss in the first half of the current year of 13.6 million pounds after exceptional charges.

Coleman, brought in last April to try and revive profits, was optimistic new ranges due to come into the stores in the autumn, including several new brands, would help improve the group's sales performance.
"We'll see some progress this year, we won't accomplish all our objectives...but we'll accomplish quite a lot."
He blamed lack of focus in marketing, quality of management and stock problems for contributing to the group's troubles.
In the past, House of Fraser's own-bought merchandise has lost out to concessions in its stores.

In the 26 weeks to January 25 like-for-like sales of own-bought ranges rose by 3.9 percent, while concessions had a 10.8 percent increase. But Coleman pointed out this was a marked improvement on the first half, when sales of own-bought items were up just one percent.
Sales overall rose 6.1 percent in the half year, including a strong performance just before Christmas and in the January sales period.
The group is testing a new low-cost store refurbishment plan costing a total of 3.7 million pounds, much more modest than the ambitious refurbishments carried soon after the group floated.
There are four new stores planned, one in Nottingham due to open in September, one in Reading, west of London, one in Solihull near Birmingham and one in Kent.
